parsed.explanation: Gender expression itself is criminalised (Penal Law arts. 265–268, Cyber Crime Law), with documented enforcement: 2018 arrests and 3–4 year sentences plus OMR 3,000 fines for cross-dressing, 2020 arrests including a foreigner, and a first-hand 2023 account of a gender-nonconforming visitor segregated at the airport, strip-exposed and touched by officers. A 2025 UPR submission reports deepening criminalisation, banned legal recognition and banned gender-affirming care, ignored recommendations, and systemic discrimination. Digital surveillance, a dual-criminality exception (art. 49) and mandatory deportation for felonies apply to visitors. No death penalty or custody torture is documented for visitors, so this sits below the 0.15 anchors, but imprisonment after discovery is documented practice, not threat.

entry_documents.exposure: Documented: a genderqueer visitor (27 Feb 2023) was held for separate examination while companions cleared immigration, made to remove her shirt and inappropriately touched. Gender-nonconformity itself triggers scrutiny regardless of home passport markers.
entry_documents.protection: Not documented. No evidence foreign documents or X markers are respected; 2013 screening proposal never implemented is the only related note.
entry_documents.interaction: Border examination feeds directly into arts. 265–266 exposure and art. 49 dual-criminality prosecution; art. 60 makes felony conviction trigger permanent deportation.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Documented: arrests for cross-dressing (2018, 2020), court sentences of 4 and 3 years plus fines; prosecution triggered by digital evidence during unrelated investigations; ISP-enabled surveillance raises discovery probability.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Not documented. No bail, counsel or release practice for visitors is recorded.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Foreign national convicted of a felony faces mandatory permanent deportation; misdemeanour conviction allows 3–15 year exclusion.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Prison placement for convicted gender-nonconforming people is explicitly not sourced; sentences are served somewhere in this system.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Unknown placement plus documented hostility of institutions leaves a detention exposure that cannot be discounted.

care_services.exposure: Gender-affirming healthcare explicitly banned (UPR submission, Aug 2025); emergency disclosure of trans status risks outing within a hostile institutional framework.
care_services.interaction: A medical emergency couples outing with criminal-exposure risk via arts. 265–266 and surveillance of records.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: State framing is threat-based: national police announce arrests of 'men in women's clothing'; gender non-conformity punished via art. 266(d); LGBT advocacy itself criminal; associations law restricts assembly.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official framing legitimises street-level hostility and reduces any expectation of protective policing.

minors_guardians.exposure: A parent travelling with a minor who is visibly gender-nonconforming risks arrest and separation; no child-specific safeguards documented.
minors_guardians.interaction: Guardian's prosecution under arts. 266/265 would leave a minor in an unaddressed custody limbo.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No trans-specific homicide or violence rate is available (explicitly not counted), so violence magnitude is undocumented; police are documented as perpetrators of arrests, not protectors.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Not documented; no anti-discrimination law exists (2025 submission recommends adopting one).
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Outing carries both social and criminal consequences; surveillance raises discovery odds in public and online.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health ignored; advocacy criminalised; systemic discrimination documented 2025.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Minimal: UPR process exists but is recorded as unheeded; the 2013 entry-screening proposal was not implemented.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Dual-criminality exception (art. 49) removes the usual foreign-national shield; thin data on prison placement and current border practice leaves unknowns that cannot be read as safety.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.15-D has documented custodial abuse, fabricated confessions and confirmed multi-year sentences for document mismatch. This dossier shares documented imprisonment for presentation and dual-criminality exposure but records no custody torture or executions, so it sits modestly above that anchor.

0.25-A involves raids, fines, brief detention with imprisonment 'rare'. Here imprisonment is documented practice with 3–4 year sentences, active national-police enforcement, digital surveillance and a first-hand border strip-examination — clearly worse, so the rating falls below 0.25.

0.35-B is discretionary stops and short releases without charge. This dossier documents court-imposed multi-year imprisonment, a dual-criminality exception and mandatory deportation — substantially more severe, so well below 0.35.

0.55-B is administrative secondary screening with refusal of entry as the worst outcome. This jurisdiction converts the same border encounter into criminal exposure for gender expression, far exceeding it.

parsed.synthesis: The combined operative regime is one system: border screening of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors (2023 first-hand account) feeds arts. 265–268 and cyber-crime provisions whose enforcement is documented with real prison sentences (2018: 3–4 years plus OMR 3,000 fines), amplified by ISP surveillance, digital-evidence-driven prosecution and art. 49's dual-criminality exception that strips foreigners of the usual shield. Art. 60 converts conviction into permanent deportation. The 2025 UPR submission confirms deepening criminalisation, banned recognition and care, ignored recommendations and systemic institutional discrimination — so no working remedy is documented. Unknown prison placement and absent violence statistics are open questions, not safety; the documented arrests, sentences and border mistreatment govern. For an adult alone or with a minor, discovery can plausibly end in imprisonment.
